stops.name: Alischanz, the second field, Gyburc's toleration and the reckoning won
stops.campa: Before the second battle Gyburc herself counsels the Christian captains to spare the defeated rather than slaughter them, heathen or not, her own crossing from one faith to the other still raw enough to make her plead for the men on the other side of the field she was born into. Willehalm's relief host breaks Tybalt's siege and wins the field this time, avenging Vivianz and holding Oransche and the whole March of Provence. It is the last war Guilhem-Willehalm will fight; from this plain the road he takes turns east and north, away from the frontier he has spent his life defending, toward Alsace and a different kind of search.

stops.name: Dôlet, the discarded manuscript of Flegetanis
stops.campa: With the march at peace, Willehalm-Kyot rides down through Spain to Toledo, the city of translators, and there, by Wolfram's own sworn account, finds the foundation of the whole adventure lying discarded, written in heathen letters. It is the starwriting of Flegetanis, the astronomer of Solomon's blood who read the name of the grail in the constellations and left it on the page for whoever could follow. Kyot has the Arabic learned in his years against the Saracens; he had to master that alphabet first, the poet says, without any art of black magic, and his baptism is what lets the writing yield.
stops.quote: Kyôt der meister wol bekant / ze Dôlet verworfen ligen vant / in heidenischer schrifte / dirre âventiure gestifte

stops.name: Anschouwe, the chronicles searched, the grail-family found
stops.campa: Flegetanis's starwriting names the grail but not its keepers, so Kyot turns scholar in his old age and hunts the Latin chronicles of the lands for a people fit to guard it. He reads Britain and elsewhere, France and Ireland, and in Anjou he finds the tale at last: the line of Mazadan set down in a book, the genealogy that runs to Titurel and Frimutel and to Herzeloyde and her sisters. The search that will end on a hillside above Arlesheim begins here among parchments, an old soldier reading his way toward the family he does not yet know he will marry into.
stops.quote: er las der lande chrônicâ / ze Britâne unt anderswâ, / ze Francrîche unt in Yrlant: / ze Anschouwe er diu mære vant

stops.name: Andlau, the wayside altar and the search begun
stops.campa: Free of the border war for the first time in years, Willehalm turns north from Anjou toward the upper Rhine, following the starwriting's hint toward a vessel called the grail. At Andlau in the Alsatian hills he keeps vigil at a wayside shrine before the last leg of the search, a stop later tradition will remember when the counts of Andlau themselves take up the grail road as their own inheritance centuries on. He carries with him the captivity-won Arabic learning that first let him read Flegetanis's starwriting, the only western man, the tradition insists, equipped to recognize what he is about to find.

stops.name: Arlesheim, the Hornikopf, Munsalvaesche found
stops.campa: On the wooded quarry-hill above Arlesheim, in a landscape the tradition later calls the terre de salvaesche, Willehalm finds the wooden grail-palace and its underground rock temple that Wolfram will name Munsalvaesche. He has followed Flegetanis's starwriting and his own years of searching to this one hillside on the edge of the Jura, and what he finds there answers both. The steel door at the temple's rear is said to yield only to one who already carries the story half-written in him. Willehalm-Kyot, soldier, monk, and now pilgrim, crosses that threshold as the last labor of a life that keeps refusing its own ending.

stops.name: Arlesheim, the marriage to Schoysiane, the grail-bearer
stops.campa: Within Munsalvaesche's household Willehalm meets Schoysiane, sister of Herzeloyde and daughter of the grail king's line, the woman the tradition names grail-bearer for the office she keeps at the temple's threshold. He marries her there, an old soldier and monk taking up a third vocation he never sought as a boy in Toulouse. It is a brief marriage measured against the length of the life that surrounds it, but the tradition holds it as the hinge of everything that follows: through Schoysiane, Willehalm-Kyot becomes kin by blood to the grail family whose secret he had until now only read about in a captured Arabic book.

stops.name: Katelangen, the dukedom and the household
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot brings his bride south again to Katelangen, the Catalan march he has held since the wars of his youth, now duke where he was once count, the frontier of his soldiering years become the seat of a different kind of life. Schoysiane keeps the household while he divides his time between the duties of the march and the grail-book he has begun, by the tradition's account, setting down in his own hand what Flegetanis wrote in the stars and what he has seen with his own eyes at Munsalvaesche. It is the shortest peace of his long life, and the tradition lets it stay unshadowed for less than two years.

stops.name: Katelangen, Schoysiane's death, Sigune's birth
stops.campa: Schoysiane dies bearing their daughter, and the tradition gives the father no long grief to speak, only the fact set down plainly the way Kyot is said to set down every hard fact of his own life: the mother lost, the child, Sigune, living. Willehalm-Kyot names her and holds the newborn in a house built for a marriage that has already ended. He is past sixty by the ordinary count of his years, a widower twice over now in different registers, monk's cowl and count's mantle and grail-bearer's husband all laid down or taken up and set aside within a single decade.

stops.name: Odilienberg, the infant Sigune given to Hohenburg
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot carries the infant Sigune north across the mountains to the Odilienberg, the holy height in Alsace where the nuns of Hohenburg keep the house Odile built two generations before, and gives the child into their fosterage rather than raise her alone on a war-worn march. From this height the whole Rhine plain opens below the convent walls, a healthier cradle by far than a dukedom bordered by raiding parties. He rides back to Katelangen without her, an old man handing the last thing his wife gave him to strangers in habits, trusting the mountain and its sisters the way he once trusted Benedict's rule at Gellone.

stops.name: Le Verdus, the second retreat
stops.campa: Willehalm-Kyot returns a last time to the hunting lodge of Le Verdus in the gorge below Gellone, the stream that gives the valley its name running past walls he built himself as a young count. He does not re-enter the abbey's cloister this time, by the tradition's account, but keeps a hermit's house at Le Verdus, apart from the brothers yet within call of the bells he endowed. Here, in the years the ordinary chronicles have already closed his book, he works at the grail-narrative in earnest: Flegetanis's starwriting, the fall and rise of Alischanz, the marriage and the loss, folded into an account he tells no one is meant to outlast him.

stops.name: Le Verdus, word of Sigune and the leash of Schionatulander
stops.campa: Word reaches the old man at Le Verdus of his daughter, grown now at Hohenburg and betrothed to a young page named Schionatulander: the strange story of a leashed hound bolting into the forest trailing a leash inscribed with a story never finished, and the boy dying in a hunt undertaken to win it back for her. Willehalm-Kyot, who has buried a wife and given away an infant, receives the report the way he has learned to receive all grief now, as material for the account he is building rather than a wound to nurse alone. The unfinished leash-text will become, centuries later, Wolfram's own unfinished Titurel.

stops.name: Le Verdus, the brother Tampenteire's death and a second niece orphaned
stops.campa: News comes south that Willehalm-Kyot's brother Tampenteire has died, leaving a daughter, Condwiramurs, without a father's protection at the age when a great house's daughters are most exposed to the ambitions of neighbors. The old man at Le Verdus, who has already raised one motherless child by proxy through the nuns of Hohenburg, takes up the office again for his brother's line. He sends word north that he will come himself rather than trust the girl's safety to letters, closing the account he has been keeping and preparing, for the first time in nearly twenty years, to leave the valley for good.
